assumptions: The account page is assumed to be an informational/self-service page rather than a step in the purchase or payment-submission flow; no route-level revenue attribution data was available to confirm this, and the weight would need to rise materially if account-page views are a required step in a subscription or renewal flow.
Traffic mix and volume are assumed steady across the window because every evaluation log line reports exactly 200 evaluations per minute; no independent traffic or conversion telemetry was inspected.

The incident is assumed to have continued past the recorded end time (21:53:36), since that timestamp corresponds to escalation and the last log lines still show the flag on and errors at 32–40%. Actual duration of customer impact is unknown.

The background `UpstreamTimeout` errors from 20:19 to 21:41 are assumed to be a pre-existing, unrelated condition, consistent with them running at baseline jitter (0–3.5%) and being unaffected by the flag.

That no deploy carried the faulty division logic during the window rests on the change record for 18:00\u201321:47 being complete; an earlier deploy introducing the latent defect was not searched for.

The two disable attempts are assumed to have failed to apply rather than to have applied and been ineffective, based on the change log recording an 'on' toggle at each disable moment. The flag system's write path was not independently verified.
input.executive_summary: For roughly six minutes late on 2 September, about a third of requests to the customer account page of the shop service failed and returned an error page. Customers trying to view their account during that window would have seen a failure on roughly one in three attempts; browsing and buying elsewhere in the shop were not affected, and no data was lost or corrupted. The cause was a newly switched-on feature that computed a spending figure and could not handle customers with no spend to divide by. Automated remediation tried twice to switch the feature back off; the switch did not actually change state and the failures continued, so the incident was handed to on-call engineers with the feature still enabled. The alert window closed at escalation, not at recovery, so account-page errors should be assumed to have continued past the stated end time until a human turned the feature off or shipped a guard around the division.
input.impact_weight_reason: Every logged failure is "account page request failed" — a self-service page for viewing account and spend information, not a cart, checkout, or payment-submission path. Nothing in the evidence shows an order or payment being rejected: the only payment-related line is a pre-existing, low-rate `UpstreamTimeout` on payment authorization that ran at 0–2% before the flag flip and is a separate condition. So this is much closer to the "account page nobody buys from" end of the scale than to checkout. It is not zero because the account page is where customers review spend and stored payment details, some of that traffic is a step on the way to a purchase or a renewal, and a hard error there in a six-minute window will send a small share of visitors away rather than back. The failure was also partial (about a third of requests) and short, so most affected visitors could retry successfully within seconds, which is why the weight sits low rather than mid-range.
input.root_cause: Enabling the `monthly-spend-feature` flag on io-shop exposed a code path on the account page that computes a ratio against a monthly-spend denominator that can be zero, so every request that evaluated the flag "on" and hit that path raised `ZeroDivisionError`. The failure mode changed identity in the exact minute the flag began evaluating "on" (21:42, mixed 97 off / 103 on) and error rate went from ~1% background `UpstreamTimeout` noise to 20–36% and stayed there while the flag remained on; no deploy is recorded in the change window, so the defect was latent in already-running code and the flag merely made it reachable. Two automated attempts to disable the flag did not take effect — the change log records an "on" write at each moment the disable was issued (21:49:54 and 21:52:48/49) and evaluation logs continued to read `monthly-spend-feature=on` through 21:53 — so the cause was wrongly marked refuted and the incident was escalated rather than mitigated.
